utterances.text: Well, let's look at the information that had been sent up, if we may, and let us take it in the sequence that you have laid out in these documents, and the first is between -- and this is the front page of 7 August 1995 to 4 September 1995. Have you reviewed these, sir?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in these there are a hundred entries that have burnings to them and 31 that do not.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And of these situation reports from 6 August to 4 September, we have approximately 740 houses partially or totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving on with your document -- by the way, sir, did you -- did you go through these and see any of the double counts that were in here?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Well, I -- I haven't found double counts to my knowledge, but it is -- may be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn to page 25, I think I just saw one. Page 25 of this document. And page 25, if we look at the -- you know, on the 30th of August at 1555?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yeah, Dukici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have Dukici, three houses burnt, and then two lines down, that's a double count.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a double one. That's a copy-paste error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And go down a little further on the 30th in Gracac. We have nine houses burnt. And if we go down one more, we have the same grid reference with nine houses burnt. That's a double count as well?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yeah. And it could have been observed by two different patrols, but, you know -- anyway, the grid reference and the day time group gives the -- out the information that you can spot out these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, just look at that grid reference. The grid reference for Gracac is the same, isn't it, WK6106?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yep. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that's clearly a double count?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just staying with this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're raising the issue of double counts which of course is a very relevant issue. Now, you have pointed out two or three double counts. The document is 70 pages. Now, what the Chamber is interested in is whether this document is disqualified by double counts, and it would assist the Chamber not only to have one or two or three or four mistakes on 70 pages, but, rather, to receive information, and it appears a matter that you could easily conclude upon with the Prosecution to say, Well, here and here we find same grid references, same number of houses, et cetera. That really assists the Chamber far more than just to have some human failure, incidentally. So if you could provide the Chamber with that, that would certainly help. That's not a comment on the relevancy of these questions, not at all, just you raised our interest in knowing more about the matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do that and it certainly is -- I understand that with the amount of information that Mr. Anttila was putting together that this happens. It just is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're all humans. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just staying with that particular issue, during that particular time frame were you reporting a much larger number of houses damaged and destroyed? I'm talking about through September of 1995.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So this particular document, just staying with the time frame 7 August 1995 through 4 September 1995, and I think from the numbers in that particular time frame it is approximately 740 damaged partially or totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: The numbers and the reports are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. But --

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: So the -- the file where you have the villages and their grid references and that information is a different file from this one, and that file was not based on these -- this information. It's based on separate visits to the village and -- villages and so on.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: So I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, but what I'm asking you is this: The information that you gave in your first iteration of this P68 that's on the screen goes from 7 August 1995 to --

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Till 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- to 4 September 1995, and in that information that you provided to the UN in Zagreb, one -- if one in Zagreb went through here they would reflect a number of 740 --

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Cases of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- damages of -- damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe the witness's testimony on direct was that this information was copied from the team sitreps which went from the teams to the HQ Sector South and not taken from the sitreps which went from Sector South to Zagreb, so I'm not sure that there's -- this document is one that was sent to Zagreb for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, the information that's in this P68 is information that was sent to Zagreb. Mr. Anttila took it out of the sitreps and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Coming from -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- systematically and put it into this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that information that was sent to Zagreb was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This information as it appears on the screen was sent to the UNMO headquarter in Zagreb as a report. Not all of this information was found on the daily sitreps sent to Zagreb. So it was gathered from the sitreps coming from the teams to the sector UNMO headquarter and then compiled and sent to Zagreb as a separate file, not as a part of a daily sitrep or daily reporting procedure to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, the information that is in these reports as we noted during this first time frame is 4 September 1995, and the information that you compiled as of 13 September 1995, and this is P98 -- and we go to -- if we can just go to the front page and get the date. If we can just shift left just a bit. And that's of -- as of 13 September, 1995, some nine days after the first iteration on violations. And can we go to the last page, page 548189. So -- if we can blow that up. So, Mr. Anttila, the information that is -- that is sent to Zagreb reflects 740 burnings, but the -- or partially damaged or damaged house, but the numbers that you compiled during that time frame are well in excess of 13.000.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. These sitreps and the clippings of the sitrep resemble the number that was observed burning by the UNMOs, and the number excess to 13.000 is a number that was found on the ground where nobody was there to observe what was going on when it was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the difference is houses that are burning and houses that are burnt?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Burning and burnt is two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you sent up the information on the burnings, but if it had been burnt you didn't send it up?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: That's gathered here on the other report, on the database where the villages are listed in and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go back to P68. And if -- let's talk about the first reference. It's in 06 at 10.30. Last line of that first insert. "The previous office of the UNMO team" -- talking about the house had been burnt to the ground.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go down two, three more on the 7th. Midway through. Midway through it says: "They saw that all buildings and cornices that seem to be demolished by artillery bombs, Lika headquarters was burnt down, and Lika Graf factory was also burned out."

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3. The third to last insert. You see that, the third to last insert starting "UNMO Headquarters," the last line: "The patrol could also observe approximately the same number of houses already burnt down."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Anttila, I think if we would go through this document, and these are just the first few pages, that often reference is made to houses burning or sometimes called houses on fire, and sometimes houses burnt, sometimes even larger numbers. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I take it that you have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to go through the whole of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. So the reports as they are on this document are reports of UNMOs observing the houses actually on fire, or in certain cases like -- like it says. When it says the houses were burnt, then they were not burning that time. You have to read it as it is on the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I think Mr. Kehoe is mainly interested in, in where you reach far higher numbers in this survey compared to this report, where your first explanation was that the smaller numbers in this report were explained by UNMOs observing houses on fire burning rather than houses burnt, that that explanation seems not to satisfy Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Okay. The -- the happenings that took place at the time were reported on the daily sitreps, and on occasions things that were observed about certain place being burnt down, or certain houses being burnt down, could be reported on a sitrep, but it was not always done that way. And that assessment was a different task from the daily reporting, to go through the villages inside the area and to report as thoroughly as possible the scale of the damages done in different -- different places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand and see whether I understood you well. What you're saying is that the burnt houses were not systematically reported in the sitreps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas there was an attempt to systematically report them in the survey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, the Human Rights Action Team leader at the time, Mr. Edward Flynn. Do you recall him?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he testified here back on April 11, 2008, page 1314, line 4: "Question: You were asked to give an estimate of the houses destroyed," and your answer is: "When I mentioned the estimate of 500 houses destroyed, I'm referring to house that were destroyed in a couple of weeks or two or three weeks after operation storm. "Answer: Yes. "Question: I understand the number is not intended to be a precise figure, but is that the general number of homes you recall during the month of August that had been burnt. "Answer: Well --" I'm just waiting to catch up, Judge. I'm trying not to go too fast. "Answer: --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought that was a signal to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was, but I missed that the interpreter in B/C/S tried to take a breath. She certainly needs one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The answer in line 12: "Answer: Well, that's my own estimate. That's my own estimate and I think I said somewhere else. I have always tried to be conservative in these estimates because I'm conscious that by exaggerating I would affect mine and others credibility. But when I gave the statement of 500, that seemed to me an entirely realistic and if anything conservative estimate of the number of buildings that had been destroyed by the end of the third week." Now, the end of the third week is almost the beginning of September. Can you tell explain to the Trial Chamber how during almost the same time frame, Mr. Flynn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it's almost 1996, isn't it? 4 and 5th plus 21 makes 25, 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think I was talking towards the end of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You said the end of the third week was almost the beginning of September. That's a way of phrasing it. We're talking about quite clearly 25th, 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, by the 25th or the 25th of August, Mr. Anttila, Mr. Flynn believes that the estimate -- estimates are approximately 500 houses. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how that number diverges so wildly -- so drastically from the 13.000-plus figure that you have set out in P98?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn did not have a chance to visit all the areas at that time, and like he said, he was being conservative, and he was talking about the numbers that he knew, that he could pinpoint out or whatever. I don't know why he came up with that number, because I don't have his mind here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I still believe on the number that the UNMO teams have reported, because it has been at that time basically more than 50 people going round in the sector doing this survey rather than just one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you were coming up with this number of 13.000 and you -- there were meetings with the HRAT teams and UNMO teams at the end of the day, were you telling Mr. Flynn about these numbers?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: We were telling that this is the number of houses being damaged. We are talking about different things that if we talk about damaged houses or burnt houses. So it's also something that by using different phrases you can -- you can get the different appearance coming out from the -- from the statement, but what we -- what I believe to the best of my knowledge is that all the UNMO teams within the sector went out to these villages and they found 13.000 houses that had been destroyed partially or totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were conveying this information to Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: KARI ANTTILA
utterances.text: That information -- I do not recall personally conveying this information to Mr. Flynn, but this report was made available for human rights teams also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to go into another area and I do believe the clock is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn for today the Chamber would like to deliver a decision and ask for the -- it will not take much time. It's actually not a decision, but these are the reasons for the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's first motion for trial-related protective measures. On the 22nd of February, 2008, the Prosecution applied for the protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion for the first witness to be called to testify in this case. According to the Prosecution, the witness's fears were objectively grounded as an atmosphere of hostility exists in Croatia towards Prosecution witnesses and towards the Croatian-Serb minority. All three Defence teams responded and requested the Chamber to deny the motion. On the 29th of February, 2008, the Prosecution sought leave to reply, which the Chamber granted. On the 6th of March, 2008, the Prosecution filed a reply to the Gotovina Defence's response. On the 13th of March, 2008, the Chamber heard the witness on the matter of protective measures. On the same day, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's application for pseudonym and voice distortion. The witness was assigned the pseudonym "Witness 136." For protective measures to be granted, the case law of this Tribunal is that the mere expression of fears by a person is not sufficient. The party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can, for example, be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. Witness 136 informed the Chamber that she does not live in Croatia but regularly travels to and through Croatia and that she has property close to Knin. She also has relatives living in Croatia. Witness 136 further informed the Chamber of comments heard by another Prosecution witness, referred to by the Prosecution as Witness 55, about potential witnesses in this case. Witness 136 and Witness 55 were former colleagues. The comments were made by Witness 55th's neighbours -- I said 55th, 55's neighbours in Croatia before the start of this trial. According to Witness 136, these comments described Witness 55's neighbours wondering which Serb witnesses were brave enough to testify in this case and whether these witnesses would dare to return to Croatia afterwards. According to Witness 136, the comments made Witness 55 unwilling to testify before the Tribunal and also instilled fear in Witness 136 for her own safety, as she drew emotional support from the fact that Witness 55 would testify in this case as well. Witness 136 stated that she had not been threatened but believed that this was due to the fact that nobody was aware that she was going to testify. The Chamber found that the Prosecution has demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of Witness 136 or her family. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness 136. We adjourn until Friday the 2nd of May, 9.00, same courtroom.
